source: Smyth and McKenna (2000) An Efficient and Effective Procedure for Updating a Competence Model for Case-Based Reasoners
finding: Competence model groups cases; the footprint set is the minimal subset giving the same coverage as the whole group. Non-footprint cases add no competence, so they are the safe ones to delete.
numbers: Two case bases: Travel (1400 cases) and Property (UCI). Solved means similarity above a threshold.
limits: Competence is defined only by the similarity threshold and a static coverage notion. It says nothing about whether a retrieved case helps or harms the final answer.
agent_relevance: Our memory could mark a stored subgoal solution as redundant if a kept one already covers the same problem region. Keep one per region.

source: Smyth and McKenna (2000) An Efficient and Effective Procedure for Updating a Competence Model for Case-Based Reasoners
finding: Updating the competence model after each new case is cheaper if only the footprint cases most similar to the new case are checked (parameter k).
numbers: Speed-up (cases examined, standard vs new) nearly 5x at 1400 cases, k=1 (20% of the comparisons). Speed-up grows with case-base size and falls about 2.5% per +1 in k. 100 random orderings per setting.
limits: Speed-up measured in comparison counts, not wall time. Two domains only.
agent_relevance: Maintenance bookkeeping can be kept cheap by looking only at nearest kept cases. Matters little for a small library.

source: Smyth and McKenna (2000) An Efficient and Effective Procedure for Updating a Competence Model for Case-Based Reasoners
finding: Accuracy of the cheaper update versus the full one is near perfect and errors accumulate slowly.
numbers: k=5 gives 100% accuracy in both domains. Travel at 1400 cases: k=3 gives 99.6% (1 case in 250 missing). k=3 accuracy fell from 99.9% at 400 cases to 99.65% at 1400 (under 4 new errors per 1000 updates).
limits: Errors compound as the base grows. Accuracy here means agreement with the full model, not with truth.
agent_relevance: Approximate dedupe is nearly as good as exact dedupe. The error is cumulative, so recheck occasionally.

source: Smyth and McKenna (2000) An Efficient and Effective Procedure for Updating a Competence Model for Case-Based Reasoners
finding: The paper frames maintenance as keeping efficiency and competence as a system evolves, and names two earlier lines: Smyth and Keane (competence-preserving deletion, a fix for the utility problem) and Minton (efficiency-based deletion). Minton's criterion is said to be inappropriate for CBR because it does not respect competence.
numbers: Qualitative statement, no numbers.
limits: Authors' own framing of rivals. Secondhand for Smyth and Keane and Minton.
agent_relevance: Deletion rules that look only at speed or only at coverage both fail. Use a rule that protects coverage and also tracks harm.

source: Smyth and Keane (1995) Remembering to forget: a competence-preserving case deletion policy for case-based reasoning systems
finding: Sorts cases into pivotal, spanning, support and auxiliary by what they cover and what covers them. Delete auxiliary cases first, then support, then spanning, pivotal last. Competence is kept while the base shrinks.
numbers: Not read this session. I recall tests on a property-valuation case base where footprint-style deletion kept accuracy up to heavy shrinkage. No figures verified.
limits: [M] memory only. Competence is a coverage proxy, tested on small, clean case bases.
agent_relevance: Basis for a rule: never drop the only case that covers a problem type.

source: Minton (1990) Quantitative results concerning the utility of explanation-based learning
finding: The utility problem: learned rules cost match time. When the cost passes the saving, the system gets slower overall. Classic reason to prune stored knowledge.
numbers: Not read. I recall PRODIGY/EBL: learned rules cut search but total solve time rose in some tests. No figures verified.
limits: [M] memory only.
agent_relevance: A bigger library is not free. Each retrieval and each prompt slot costs tokens and attention.

source: Francis and Ram (1993) The utility problem in case-based reasoning
finding: Names the swamping problem in CBR: as cases grow, retrieval cost overtakes the benefit.
numbers: Not read. Cited in the Memento paper as the origin of swamping. No figures.
limits: [M] and secondhand via Memento.
agent_relevance: Swamping is the expected failure of a never-pruned library.

source: Zhu and Yang (1999) Case addition policy for case-based reasoning
finding: Keep a new case only if it adds coverage; a probabilistic estimate of competence guides addition. Cited by Smyth and McKenna as the addition side of maintenance.
numbers: Not read. No figures verified.
limits: [M]. Cited via the Smyth and McKenna text I opened.
agent_relevance: Retain only when the new solved item covers something the library does not.

source: Wilson and Martinez (2000) Reduction techniques for instance-based learning algorithms
finding: Large comparison of instance pruning methods (ENN, RENN, DROP1-5 and others) on many UCI sets. Noise filtering and pruning can cut storage a lot at small accuracy cost; DROP3/DROP4 were among the best.
numbers: Not read this session. From memory: 30+ datasets, storage cut by a large share for the best methods, accuracy loss about 1-2 points. Treat as unverified.
limits: [M]. Numbers unverified. Tabular data, k-NN, not LLM agents.
agent_relevance: Strong prior: most stored items can go with little loss, if the kept ones cover the space.

source: Delany and Cunningham (2004) An analysis of case-base editing in a spam filtering system
finding: Case-base editing on email spam filtering: competence-based editing and noise removal shrink the base and often keep or raise accuracy; concept drift means old cases go stale and need forgetting.
numbers: Not opened (fetch returned a stub page); only a search listing seen. No figures.
limits: [M]. Spam-specific. Drift makes age a real factor.
agent_relevance: Age-based decay matters when the task distribution drifts, less when problem types are stable.

source: Leake and Wilson (2001) Maintaining case-based reasoners: dimensions and directions
finding: Framework: maintenance can target different knowledge containers (cases, indexes, similarity, adaptation) and run on different schedules (continuous, periodic, on demand), online or offline.
numbers: Not read. No numbers.
limits: [M]. Conceptual.
agent_relevance: Decide what to maintain (items, retrieval keys, similarity) and when (after each task vs in batches). Our loop can batch.

source: Smyth and McKenna (2001) Competence models and the maintenance problem
finding: Journal version of the competence model. Gives the groupings and the claim that footprint sets drive deletion, addition and retrieval.
numbers: Not opened. Seen only in a search listing.
agent_relevance: Same as the 2000 model.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior
finding: Adding every experience hurts. Adding only checked-good experiences helps. Tested on four agents with kNN-retrieved past runs.
numbers: Success rate or accuracy, memory size in brackets. RegAgent: fixed 67.53, add-all 55.48 (4100), strict 70.95 (2938). EHRAgent: fixed 16.75, add-all 13.05, strict 38.50. AgentDriver: fixed 40.11, add-all 32.32, strict 51.00. CIC-IoT: fixed 71.50, add-all 59.90, strict 85.40.
limits: Strict means a ground-truth oracle. Four agents, some synthetic. Other LLM backbones checked in appendix only.
agent_relevance: Never store a solved subgoal without a check. Add-all lost 8 to 12 points against doing nothing.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior
finding: A weak LLM judge gives mixed gains. A judge tuned on only 300 correct trajectories did much better. A vanilla judge can do worse than a small fixed memory.
numbers: Coarse judges C1/C2/C3. EHRAgent: 26.19 / 32.21 / 34.66. AgentDriver: 36.92 / 40.01 / 47.37. CIC-IoT: 74.00 / 68.80 / 79.50. RegAgent: C1 63.18 and C2 65.78 sit below fixed 67.53.
limits: C3 is fine-tuned on 300 items per agent. A tuned judge may not transfer.
agent_relevance: The quality of the checker sets the ceiling for retention. Invest in the checker before the store.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior
finding: Experience following: when a new query is close to a stored query, the output copies the stored output. So a bad stored case spreads errors.
numbers: Output similarity tracks input similarity, correlation near 1 (Pearson r about 1) under add-all. Under the fixed memory both similarities stay lower and the agent relies more on its own reasoning.
limits: Similarity measured per agent by feature or embedding distance. Correlational.
agent_relevance: This is the main harm path for a case library: a wrong close case gets copied. Need harm tracking, not only success tracking.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior
finding: Deleting records by measured future utility (history-based) beats timed or frequency deletion when the utility checker is reliable. Periodic deletion shrinks memory with little loss.
numbers: Strict evaluator, no deletion: Reg 70.95 / EHR 38.67 / Driver 51.00 / IoT 85.40. History-based: Reg 67.65 (949) / EHR 42.06 (784) / Driver 51.81 (846) / IoT 89.60 (788). Combined: EHR 42.34 (248), IoT 85.50 (188). Periodic: Reg 69.80, IoT 80.80.
limits: History-based deletion needs at least n retrievals per record. With the coarse C1 judge: Reg 59.32, IoT 68.80, below no deletion (63.18 and 74.00) in those cells, so gains need a reliable judge. Table cell alignment in the PDF text is partly garbled. Authors report an average gain near 10% for add plus delete vs naive growth.
agent_relevance: Delete a stored item when its average downstream outcome across several retrievals is bad. Use at least a few retrievals before judging.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior
finding: Records that pass the add filter can still mislead later (misaligned experience replay). History-based deletion removes them.
numbers: With a strict evaluator in AgentDriver, history-based deletion even beat an error-free memory baseline. With C1 on EhrAgent, retained records were 44.1% correct vs deleted 36.3%; with C3 54.8 vs 48.2. On CIC-IoT retained 78.9 vs deleted 56.7 (C1).
limits: The deleted-vs-retained gap is small for EhrAgent, and for AgentDriver with GPT-4o-mini the retained set was lower in quality than the deleted set.
agent_relevance: A case can be correct yet harmful for a different problem. Track per-use harm.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior
finding: The policies still help under a hard memory cap and under task distribution shift.
numbers: Under a size cap the agent kept high performance versus fixed memory (Figure 17, no table read). Under task shift, combined deletion with strict add passed its error-free variant near task index 1000 (appendix).
limits: Numbers only in figures. Shift was simulated by reordering test sets.
agent_relevance: Supports a capped library with utility-based eviction.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: ExpeL keeps both raw successful trajectories (retrieved by task similarity) and distilled insights. Insights are edited with ADD, UPVOTE, DOWNVOTE and EDIT; one whose importance count reaches zero is deleted.
numbers: HotpotQA: insights-only 36%, retrieve-only 31%. ALFWorld: insights-only 50%, retrieve-only 55%. WebShop: 37% vs 38%. ExpeL 40% vs Reflexion 39% (HotpotQA); ALFWorld 54% vs 59%.
limits: Rule-based importance counts are heuristic. Only text environments. Gains vary by domain.
agent_relevance: A vote-count rule gives cheap pruning of abstract rules. Keeping both raw cases and rules beat either alone.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: Ablations: more gathered experience helps; selection by task similarity beats random; reflections added to insight extraction hurt.
numbers: HotpotQA insights: hand-crafted about 29%, with reflections 28%, gpt-3.5 insights 32%, ExpeL 39%. ALFWorld retrieval: random 40%, reasoning-similarity 48.5%, task-similarity (ExpeL) 59%.
limits: Row-to-value alignment in the extracted table is garbled; values read as the paper's Table 3 text describes them. Standard errors 0.3 to 2.1.
agent_relevance: Which case you retrieve matters as much as what you store. Do not mix noisy reflections into stored lessons.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Reusable workflows induced from successful runs raise web-agent success. Online mode keeps only runs a judge calls successful.
numbers: WebArena (812 tasks): +12.0 absolute points, 51.1% relative over BrowserGym. Mind2Web cross-task: 24.6% relative step success. Gap rises to 22.5 points after tens of examples in online mode.
limits: Judge errors give wrong workflows that hurt; authors say so. WebArena has repeated task templates, which inflates in-template gains.
agent_relevance: Retain after a success check, and store the abstract recipe not the full transcript.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Cross-template test: gains hold when tasks do not share a template.
numbers: Cross-template subset: AWM 33.2 total success vs AutoEval 23.2 and BrowserGym 20.5 per the table text.
limits: Table is garbled in the PDF text. Subset is small, tens of tasks per website.
agent_relevance: Evidence against the worry that stored items only help near-duplicates, but weak.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Agentic Context Engineering
finding: Context collapse: asking the model to rewrite the whole stored context each time wiped it out. Incremental small updates with a non-LLM merge and dedupe avoided this.
numbers: On AppWorld, at step 60 context had 18,282 tokens and 66.7 accuracy; next step it was 122 tokens at 57.1, below the 63.7 no-adaptation baseline.
limits: One case study of a baseline method. The ACE benefit reported is +10.6% on agents, +8.6% on finance.
agent_relevance: Never let the model regenerate the whole library in one pass. Edit item by item.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Agentic Context Engineering
finding: Grow-and-refine: new items are appended, existing ones updated in place with counters, then a de-dup step prunes near-duplicates by similarity.
numbers: Ablation, AppWorld: ReAct alone 63.7 (normal-test TGC); ACE offline 72.0; online 76.2 with offline warmup variants. Dropping the reflector or multi-epoch lowers the gains.
limits: Table text is garbled. Authors state gains need a reasonably strong reflector, and short tasks like HotPotQA or Game of 24 need only brief rules.
agent_relevance: Counters plus dedupe is a workable maintenance policy for a lesson list.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Agentic Context Engineering
finding: Robustness: ACE degrades gracefully with noisy reflections, staying above base except under fully adversarial updates every iteration.
numbers: Reported qualitatively in the main text; appendix A.4 not read.
limits: Appendix not opened.
agent_relevance: The library can tolerate some bad entries if updates are incremental.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank: scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory
finding: Storing lessons from failures as well as successes helps, while two success-only baselines did not gain or even lost when failures were added.
numbers: WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash. Synapse 40.6 (success only) to 41.7 (with failures). AWM 44.4 to 42.2. ReasoningBank 46.5 to 49.7. Headline: up to 20% relative gain, up to 16% fewer steps.
limits: One subset and one backbone for this ablation. The paper's own consolidation was add-only with no pruning.
agent_relevance: Direct answer to whether storing only successes loses useful traps: it can. Keep lessons from failures as distilled warnings.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank: scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory
finding: Robust to a noisy success/failure judge across a wide range.
numbers: Judge accuracy against ground truth was 72.7%. Simulated accuracy from 100% to 50%: success rates in a narrow band around 47.6 to 53 (read from figure text); 70 to 90% accuracy gave similar rates, 100% best.
limits: Figure values read from garbled text. Contrasts with Xiong et al., where weak judges hurt.
agent_relevance: Papers disagree on judge noise: abstract lessons seem to tolerate noise more than raw trajectories.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank: scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory
finding: Authors kept consolidation to plain addition on purpose and flag pruning as future work.
numbers: Text says newly generated items are directly added without additional pruning.
limits: So ReasoningBank gives no evidence on pruning itself.
agent_relevance: Gap in the literature: no test of pruning on a distilled lesson bank.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs
finding: More retrieved cases do not keep helping: performance peaks around K=4 retrieved cases and then flattens or dips.
limits: Gain from K=1 to K=4 is under 1 point on average, so small. Single benchmark.
agent_relevance: Show only a few cases per prompt. The first case gives most of the gain (+5.7 PM).

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Case bank saturates; no performance drop found with growth, and the authors name swamping as a risk for systems that keep adding without curation.
numbers: Authors looked for drops along the learning curve and found none. About 3k training items; marginal gains after a few iterations. Case memory adds 4.7 to 9.6 absolute points on out-of-distribution tasks.
limits: Finite closed benchmark with 3k items; authors say this is why swamping did not appear. Not a test of pruning.
agent_relevance: A failed attempt to show swamping at 3k cases. Swamping may need far bigger libraries; do not prune on size alone early.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: test-time learning with adaptive memory
finding: Curated compact memory beats appending the full history, which can fall below the no-memory baseline.
numbers: AIME 2024: Claude 3.5 Sonnet full-history 26.7% vs curated (DC) 50.0%. GPT-4o baseline 20.0%, full-history 6.7%, DC-RS 40.0%. Claude on GPQA-Diamond 59.6% to 68.7% (DC-RS); retrieval only (DR) 63.6%.
limits: AIME sets are tiny (30 questions each), so one question is 3.3 points. GPT-4o on GPQA gained only 57.1 to 58.1; retrieval of weak examples caused confusion.
agent_relevance: Strong direct evidence that curation, not just storage, drives gains. Uncurated storage can hurt below zero.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: test-time learning with adaptive memory
finding: Small models gain little because they curate and retrieve badly.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Haiku AIME 2024: baseline 10.0, DC-Cu 36.7, DC-RS 30.0; GPQA-Diamond 43.4 baseline, DC- 41.9, DC-RS 49.0. GPT-4o-mini showed even smaller gains (not tabulated here).
limits: Haiku gains were mixed across sets. Result depends on model size.
agent_relevance: The curation step needs a capable model. Do not hand it to a weak one.

source: Chhikara et al. (2025) Mem0: building production-ready AI agents with scalable long-term memory
finding: An LLM decides per fact to ADD, UPDATE, DELETE or do nothing against existing memories. Distilled memories beat chunk retrieval but not full context.
numbers: LLM-as-judge on LoCoMo: best RAG about 61%, Mem0 67%, Mem0g over 68%, full context about 73%. p95 latency 1.44 s for Mem0 vs about 17 s full context (92% lower).
limits: Authors' own system, own re-runs of baselines. Full context won on accuracy. Conversations average 26k tokens, short enough to fit.
agent_relevance: Distilling and updating costs a few points but cuts cost a lot; the choice depends on whether the library will outgrow the context.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) MemoryBank: enhancing LLMs with long-term memory
finding: Ebbinghaus-style decay: memory strength S rises by 1 and the clock resets each time an item is recalled; retention R = exp(-t/S). Old, unused items fade.
numbers: Method text read (formula only). I did not read evaluation numbers.
limits: Time decay is borrowed from human memory and not shown here to beat other rules. Memento's text cites it as an example, not a validated result.
agent_relevance: A cheap eviction rule, but no measured comparison against utility-based deletion found.

source: Evidence gap note (this search)
finding: I found no study that compares footprint or coverage pruning with utility-based pruning on an LLM agent library. Classical work tests coverage on k-NN or CBR sets. LLM work tests judge quality and utility deletion. The two have not met.
numbers: Web search budget ended after about 5 searches; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned rate limits.
limits: Absence in what I could reach; the literature may hold more.
agent_relevance: Candidate experiment for us: coverage dedupe vs harm-based eviction on the same library.
